Bifurcating solutions in a non-homogeneous boundary value problem for a nonlinear pendulum equation.

Fernando P. da Costa Address: Departamento de Ciências e Tecnologia, Universidade Aberta, Lisboa, Portugal, and Centre for Mathematical Analysis, Geometry, and Dynamical Systems, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal Email address: fcosta@uab.pt , Michael Grinfeld Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Strathclyde, Glasgow, United Kingdom Email address: m.grinfeld@strath.ac.uk , João T. Pinto Address: Departamento de Matemática, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal, and Centre for Mathematical Analysis, Geometry, and Dynamical Systems, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal Email address: jpinto@math.tecnico.ulisboa.pt and Kedtysack Xayxanadasy Address: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Natural Sciences, National University of Laos, Dongdok Campus, Vientiane, Laos Email address: kedtysack@gmail.com
Date: July 29, 2019
Abstract.

Motivated by recent studies of bifurcations in liquid crystals cells [1, 2] we consider a nonlinear pendulum ordinary differential equation in the bounded interval (−L,L)(-L,L) with non-homogeneous mixed boundary conditions (Dirichlet an one end of the interval, Neumann at the other) and study the bifurcation diagram of its solutions having as bifurcation parameter the size of the interval, 2​L2L, and using techniques from phase space analysis, time maps, and asymptotic estimation of integrals, complemented by appropriate numerical evidence.

Key words and phrases: 
Non-homogeneous two-points boundary value problems; Bifurcations; Nonlinear pendulum; Asymptotic evaluation of integrals.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 34B15, 34C23; Secondary 41A60.

1. Introduction

Motivated by the study of the twist-Fréedericksz transition in a nematic liquid crystal cell, a non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary value problem for the nonlinear pendulum equation

(1) x′′​(t)+sin⁡2​x​(t)=0,x^{\prime\prime}(t)+\sin 2x(t)=0,

for tt in the interval [−L,L],[-L,L], was considered in recent papers [1, 2], and the structure of the bifurcating solutions when the parameter LL is changed was studied.

In this paper we consider again the existence of solutions for a non-homogeneous boundary value problem for equation (1), this time with a Dirichlet condition at t=−Lt=-L and a Neumann one at t=L,t=L, a case that may be relevant for modelling the twist-Fréedericksz transition in a cholesteric liquid crystal cell [4]. The problem that will be considered is the following, illustrated in Figure 1,

(2) {x′=yy′=−sin⁡2​x,\displaystyle\begin{cases}x^{\prime}=y\\ y^{\prime}=-\sin 2x,\end{cases}
(3) ​x​(−L)=−ϕ,y⁡(L)=ϕ⋆.\displaystyle\rule{0.0pt}{14.22636pt}x(-L)=-\phi,\qquad y(L)=\phi^{\star}.

where ϕ⋆:=1−cos⁡2​ϕ.\phi^{\star}:=\sqrt{1-\cos 2\phi}.

System (2) has a first integral given by

(4) V⁡(x,y)=y2−cos⁡2​x.V(x,y)=y^{2}-\cos 2x.

and from V⁡(−ϕ,0)=V⁡(0,ϕ⋆)V(-\phi,0)=V(0,\phi^{\star}) we conclude that the points (−ϕ,0)(-\phi,0) and (0,ϕ⋆)(0,\phi^{\star}) lie on the same orbit of (2), as illustrated in Figure 1 by the orbit denoted by γ∗\gamma*. This relation between the conditions imposed at the two boundary points entails a certain symmetry in the allowed solutions, akin to what happened in the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions studied in [1], and is a reasonable first step towards the understanding of the general case.

The tools used in this paper are based on appropriately defined time maps, measuring the time spent by a given orbit between two of its points. According to what will be most appropriate for the computations, we will identify an orbit by the ordinate of its first intersection either with the xx-axis, the yy-axis, or the line x=−ϕx=-\phi, leading to different, although equivalent, time maps.

We study the bifurcation diagram of solutions to (2)–(3) using the following procedure: we start by identifying a segment of an orbit of (2), γ∗\gamma^{*}, such that the corresponding solution, in addition to satisfying the boundary conditions (3), x⁡(−L)=−ϕx(-L)=-\phi and y⁡(L)=ϕ∗y(L)=\phi^{*}, also satisfies y⁡(−L)=0y(-L)=0 and x⁡(L)=0x(L)=0 (see Figure 1). We call the solution corresponding to γ∗\gamma^{*} a critical solution (and γ∗\gamma^{*} a critical (segment of an) orbit). Calling this solution critical is justified as we will prove that in bifurcation diagrams parameterized by LL, there is more than one solution branch passing through it. To this (segment of) orbit γ∗\gamma^{*} corresponds a critical time T∗T^{*}, and a corresponding critical value of L=L∗=T∗/2>0.L=L^{*}=T^{*}/2>0.

We then perturb this (segment of) orbit and investigate how the time spent changes relative to T∗T^{*}. This time is measured by adequately defined time maps, whose definition arises naturally from the phase portrait and the first integral (4) (see, e.g. [3, 6]). This approach was used in [1, 2] for the study of (2) with non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions; its application in the present case led to some unexpected difficulties and the analytical study had to be completed with numerical simulations providing solid evidence for a conjecture about the existence of a single minimum of the time maps of some solution branches.

2. Time maps: definition and basic results

For every α∈(0,π2)\alpha\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right), the orbit γα\gamma_{\alpha} of (2) that intersects the xx-axis at (−α,0)(-\alpha,0) is periodic. Using (2) and the first integral (4) the time taken from the point of intersection of γα\gamma_{\alpha} with the negative-xx semi-axis, (−α,0),(-\alpha,0), to the first intersection with the positive-yy semi-axis, occurring at the point (0,2​sin⁡α),(0,\sqrt{2}\sin\alpha), is given by the following time map

(5) T⁡(α):=∫0α1cos⁡2​x−cos⁡2​α​𝑑x.T(\alpha):=\int_{0}^{\alpha}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos 2x-\cos 2\alpha}}dx.

We will also need to measure the time taken by γα\gamma_{\alpha} described above between its point of intersection with the positive-yy semi-axis, (0,2​sin⁡α),(0,\sqrt{2}\sin\alpha), and the point of its first intersection with the vertical line x=νx=\nu, with ν∈(0,π2).\nu\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}). In the same way as above, the fact that (4) is a first integral allows us to conclude that this time is given by the time map

(6) T1​(α,ν):=∫0ν1cos⁡2​x−cos⁡2​α​𝑑x.T_{1}(\alpha,\nu):=\int_{0}^{\nu}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos 2x-\cos 2\alpha}}dx.

Observe that T1​(ϕ,ϕ)=T⁡(ϕ).T_{1}(\phi,\phi)=T(\phi).

The proof of the following result can be consulted in [1].

Proposition 1.

Let 0<ϕ<α<π2.0<\phi<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}. The time maps TT and T1T_{1} defined by (5) and (6), respectively, satisfy:

  1. (1)

    α↦T⁡(α)\alpha\mapsto T(\alpha) is strictly increasing, and converges to +∞+\infty as α→π2\alpha\to\frac{\pi}{2} and to π2​2\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} as α→0.\alpha\to 0.

  2. (2)

    α↦T1​(α,ϕ)\alpha\mapsto T_{1}(\alpha,\phi) is strictly decreasing.

To study the orbits located above the homoclinic orbit to (π2,0)≡(−π2,0)(\tfrac{\pi}{2},0)\equiv(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},0) in the positive-yy semi-plane we use as an identifying parameter its intersection with some positive line (instead of the parameter α\alpha above that in these cases is nonexistent, since these orbits do no intersect the xx-axis). In [1, 2] the parameter used in these cases was the ordinate β\beta of the intersection of the orbit with the positive-yy semi-axis. Here we shall use as parameter the value z=y​(−L)2z=y(-L)^{2}, i.e., the square of the intersection of the orbit with the vertical line x=−ϕx=-\phi, or, in terms of the original boundary value problem, the square of the value of the derivative of the solution x⁡(t)x(t) at the boundary point t=−Lt=-L. For orbits intersecting the xx-axis we can easily relate the parameters α\alpha and zz using the first integral (4): V⁡(−α,0)=V⁡(−ϕ,z).V(-\alpha,0)=V(-\phi,\sqrt{z}). In order not to overload the notation we shall use the same symbols, TT or T1T_{1}, for the time maps independently of which variable, α\alpha or zz, is being used in the parametrization of the orbits.

3. Phase space analysis of orbits bifurcating from γ∗\gamma^{*}

Let γ∗\gamma^{*} be the orbit of (2)–(3) shown in Figure 1. Let T∗=2​L∗T^{*}=2L^{*} be the time taken by this orbit. This orbit rests on the periodic orbit of (2) intersecting the negative xx-axis at x=−ϕ.x=-\phi. Slightly perturbing this supporting periodic orbit to another whose intersection with the negative xx-axis is at −α<−ϕ-\alpha<-\phi, with α−ϕ\alpha-\phi sufficiently small, we easily conclude from the phase portrait and from the continuous dependence of solutions of ODEs on the initial data over finite time intervals, that there exists four distinct orbits satisfying (2)–(3) for appropriately chosen values of LL close to L∗L^{*}. We shall denote these as solutions of type II, AA, BB, and CC, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Taking into account the time maps defined in Section 2 the time spent in each orbit of the above types is given by, respectively,

(7) TI​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{I}(\alpha,\phi) :⁣=\displaystyle:= T1​(α,ϕ)−T1​(α,x⋆)\displaystyle T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)-T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})
(8) TA​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{A}(\alpha,\phi) :⁣=\displaystyle:= 2​T​(α)−(T1​(α,ϕ)+T1​(α,x⋆))\displaystyle 2T(\alpha)-\left(T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)+T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})\right)
(9) TB​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{B}(\alpha,\phi) :⁣=\displaystyle:= T1​(α,ϕ)+T1​(α,x⋆)\displaystyle T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)+T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})
(10) TC​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{C}(\alpha,\phi) :⁣=\displaystyle:= 2​T​(α)−(T1​(α,ϕ)−T1​(α,x⋆))\displaystyle 2T(\alpha)-\left(T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)-T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})\right)

where x⋆x^{\star} is the positive solution of V⁡(x⋆,ϕ⋆)=V⁡(−α,0),V(x^{\star},\phi^{\star})=V(-\alpha,0), i.e.,

(11) x⋆=x⋆​(α,ϕ):=12​arccos⁡(1−cos⁡2​ϕ+cos⁡2​α).x^{\star}=x^{\star}(\alpha,\phi):=\frac{1}{2}\arccos(1-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2\alpha).

From the phase portraits in figures 1 and 2 we conclude that orbits of type AA and CC can be continued down to −α↓−π2-\alpha\downarrow-\frac{\pi}{2}, which corresponds to their initial point converging to points on the homoclinic orbit to (−π2,0)≡(π2,0)(-\frac{\pi}{2},0)\equiv(\frac{\pi}{2},0) in {y<0},\{y<0\}, but not further down: if the initial point gets to, or below, this homoclinic orbit the corresponding orbit remains in {y<0}\{y<0\}, and the solution will not satisfy the boundary condition y⁡(L)=ϕ⋆>0y(L)=\phi^{\star}>0, for any value of LL.

In contradistinction with these cases, in principle there is no obstruction to orbits of types II and BB to be continued above the homoclinic orbit to (−π2,0)≡(π2,0)(-\frac{\pi}{2},0)\equiv(\frac{\pi}{2},0) in {y>0}.\{y>0\}. To properly handle this possibility it is convenient to parameterize the orbits, and the corresponding time maps, not by α\alpha but by either the ordinate of its intersection with the positive yy-axis, β\beta, or by the ordinate of its initial point y⁡(−L)y(-L), or, as we shall use in Section 4.4, by the square of this quantity z:=y​(−L)2z:=y(-L)^{2}. Using these parameterizations the variable α\alpha in the function x⋆x^{\star} needs to be correspondingly changed to β\beta, y⁡(−L)y(-L), or zz, which is easily done using the fact that VV is a first integral to relate the various parameters, V⁡(−α,0)=V⁡(0,β)=V⁡(−ϕ,y⁡(−L))=V⁡(−ϕ,z),V(-\alpha,0)=V(0,\beta)=V(-\phi,y(-L))=V(-\phi,\sqrt{z}), leading to the corresponding expressions for x⋆x^{\star}. One that we shall frequently use in what follows is the expression in terms of zz:

(12) x¯⋆​(z):=12​arccos⁡(1−z).\bar{x}^{\star}(z):=\frac{1}{2}\arccos(1-z).

Notwithstanding the possibility of these orbits to be continued above the homoclinic, they cannot be continued for arbitrarily large values of y⁡(−L)y(-L), although for different reasons, as we shall see below.

Type II orbits obviously cease to exist when y⁡(−L)=ϕ⋆y(-L)=\phi^{\star}, since, when this occurs, the initial and final points of the orbit coincide (see Figure 3.)

The reason why these orbits cannot be continued above this value of y⁡(−L)y(-L) is easy to understand from the phase portrait: since the initial and final points of type II orbits are always regular points of the phase plane, having y⁡(−L)y(-L) approaching the limit value ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} we have type II orbits taking less and less time 2​L2L, with L→0L\to 0 as y⁡(−L)→ϕ⋆y(-L)\to\phi^{\star}, and thus (2)–(3) having no sense in the limit. In fact, analysis of the time maps tell us exactly the same: taking z→(ϕ⋆)2z\to(\phi^{\star})^{2} in (7) (with the variable zz instead of α\alpha) and noting that, by (12) and the definition of ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}, limz→(ϕ⋆)2x¯⋆​(z)=ϕ\displaystyle{\lim_{z\to(\phi^{\star})^{2}}\bar{x}^{\star}(z)=\phi}, it immediately follows that TI​(z)→0T_{I}(z)\to 0. In section 4.1 a study of the monotonicity of TIT_{I} will be presented.

The situation for type BB orbits is more interesting. Since all orbits of (2) above the orbit homoclinic to (−π2,0)≡(π2,0)(-\frac{\pi}{2},0)\equiv(\frac{\pi}{2},0) in {y>0}\{y>0\} have an absolute minimum at x=π2x=\frac{\pi}{2}, there are no type BB orbits resting on an orbit of (2) if the yy-component of that minimum is bigger that ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}, since in this case no segment of the orbit (and in particular the one we call type BB orbit) can satisfy the boundary condition y⁡(L)=ϕ⋆y(L)=\phi^{\star}. Using the first integral VV this means that the largest value of y⁡(−L)y(-L) that a type BB orbit must satisfy is given by V⁡(−ϕ,y⁡(−L))=V⁡(π2,ϕ⋆)V(-\phi,y(-L))=V(\frac{\pi}{2},\phi^{\star}), and so, from ϕ⋆=1−cos⁡2​ϕ,\phi^{\star}=\sqrt{1-\cos 2\phi}, we must have y⁡(−L)=2,y(-L)=\sqrt{2}, independently of ϕ.\phi. This implies that orbits of type BB only exist for y⁡(−L)∈(0,2]y(-L)\in(0,\sqrt{2}].

To understand what is going on in this case we observe that, due to the periodicity of the vector field, for initial points (−ϕ,y⁡(−L))(-\phi,y(-L)) with y⁡(−L)y(-L) bigger than the ordinate of the point on the homoclinic orbit (but less than 2\sqrt{2}), there is another orbit with end point (−x⋆,ϕ⋆)(-x^{\star},\phi^{\star}). This orbit is part of a new class of orbits we shall call type B′B^{\prime}. See Figure 4.

When y⁡(−L)→2y(-L)\to\sqrt{2} the two end points of orbits of types BB and B′B^{\prime} converge to one another and at y⁡(−L)=2y(-L)=\sqrt{2} the two coincide with the point (π2,ϕ⋆)(\frac{\pi}{2},\phi^{\star}), and both cease to exist for y⁡(−L)>2.y(-L)>\sqrt{2}.

4. Bifurcation diagram of orbits bifurcating from γ⋆\gamma^{\star}

To draw the bifurcation diagram of orbits bifurcating from γ⋆\gamma^{\star} we need to put together the information in Section 3, gathered from the phase portrait, with information about the time spent by each orbit, obtained from the study of the time maps, which we will do next.

4.1. Behavior of type II solutions branch

We first consider solutions of type II. From 7, the definition of the time maps (5) and (6), and Proposition 1, we conclude that

TI​(α,ϕ)=T1​(α,ϕ)−T1​(α,x⋆)<T1​(α,ϕ)<T1​(ϕ,ϕ)=T⁡(ϕ)=T∗=2​L∗.T_{I}(\alpha,\phi)=T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)-T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})<T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)<T_{1}(\phi,\phi)=T(\phi)=T^{*}=2L^{*}.

Thus, in the bifurcation diagram plotted using the time spent by the orbit as the bifurcation parameter, type II branch of solutions exist to the left of the bifurcation point T∗T^{*} correspondent to the critical orbit γ⋆.\gamma^{\star}. Let us compute the derivative ∂TI/∂α.\partial T_{I}/\partial\alpha. From

∂TI∂α​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle\frac{\partial T_{I}}{\partial\alpha}(\alpha,\phi) =\displaystyle= ∂T1∂α​(α,ϕ)−∂T1∂α​(α,x⋆)−∂T1∂x⋆​d​x⋆d​α\displaystyle\frac{\partial T_{1}}{\partial\alpha}(\alpha,\phi)-\frac{\partial T_{1}}{\partial\alpha}(\alpha,x^{\star})-\frac{\partial T_{1}}{\partial x^{\star}}\frac{dx^{\star}}{d\alpha}
=\displaystyle= −∫x⋆​(α)ϕsin⁡2​α(cos⁡2​x−cos⁡2​ϕ)32dx\displaystyle-\int_{x^{\star}(\alpha)}^{\phi}\frac{\sin 2\alpha}{(\cos 2x-\cos 2\phi)^{\frac{3}{2}}}dx
−2​sin⁡2​αcos⁡2​x⋆​(α)−cos⁡2​ϕ​1−(1−cos⁡2​ϕ−cos⁡2​α)2,\displaystyle\!\!-\;\frac{2\sin 2\alpha}{\sqrt{\cos 2x^{\star}(\alpha)-\cos 2\phi}\sqrt{1-(1-\cos 2\phi-\cos 2\alpha)^{2}}},

we conclude that ∂TI/∂α<0\partial T_{I}/\partial\alpha<0, since it is clear from the definition of type II solutions that we always have x⋆<ϕx^{\star}<\phi (see Figure 3). This means that the branch of type II solutions in the bifurcation diagram has no turning points.

The above computations were done using the parametrization of orbits by the parameter α\alpha, and thus the corresponding orbits are inside the region bounded by the homoclinics. This is always the case when (−ϕ,ϕ⋆)(-\phi,\phi^{\star}) is in this region. When it is outside this region the orbits can still be continued, as explained in Section 3, and the results above still hold using a parametrization of the orbits by either of the parameters introduced therein, namely y⁡(−L),zy(-L),z, or β\beta.

The results above and the discussion in Section 3 allows us to conclude that the type II solutions branch continues monotonically to T=0T=0, as shown in Figure 7.

4.2. Behavior of type CC solutions branch

Consider now solutions of type CC. From (10), the definition of the time maps (5) and (6), and Proposition 1, we conclude that

TC​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{C}(\alpha,\phi) =\displaystyle= 2​T​(α)+T1​(α,x⋆)−T1​(α,ϕ)\displaystyle 2T(\alpha)+T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})-T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)
=\displaystyle= T⁡(α)+T1​(α,x⋆)⏟>0+(T⁡(α)−T1​(α,ϕ))⏟>0\displaystyle T(\alpha)+\underbrace{T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star})}_{>0}+\underbrace{\bigl(T(\alpha)-T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)\bigr)}_{>0}
>\displaystyle> T⁡(α)\displaystyle T(\alpha)
>\displaystyle> T⁡(ϕ)=T∗=2​L∗.\displaystyle T(\phi)=T^{*}=2L^{*}.

In the other hand, since by (7) and (10) we can write TC​(α)=2​T​(α)−TI​(α)T_{C}(\alpha)=2T(\alpha)-T_{I}(\alpha), we conclude that

∂TC∂α​(α,ϕ)=2​T′​(α)−∂TI∂α​(α,ϕ)>0,\frac{\partial T_{C}}{\partial\alpha}(\alpha,\phi)=2T^{\prime}(\alpha)-\frac{\partial T_{I}}{\partial\alpha}(\alpha,\phi)>0,

where the positivity comes from Proposition 1 and the result in Section 4.1. Note that orbits of type CC are always inside the region bounded by the homoclinics and so this analysis is enough to conclude that, like the branch of type II solutions, the type CC solutions branch do not have turning points and, from Proposition 1.(1), exists globally when L→+∞L\to+\infty, since type CC orbits take progressively longer times as α→π/2.\alpha\to\pi/2..

4.3. Local behavior of type BB solutions branch

In this section we study the behavior of the solution branch of type BB solutions locally close to the bifurcation point.

Consider the branch of bifurcating solutions of (2)–(3) denoted by BB in Section 3. As already observed, the time spent by an orbit of type BB is given by

(13) TB​(α,ϕ)=T1​(α,ϕ)+T1​(α,x⋆​(α)),T_{B}(\alpha,\phi)=T_{1}(\alpha,\phi)+T_{1}(\alpha,x^{\star}(\alpha)),

where T1T_{1} is the time map defined by (6) and x⋆x^{\star} is defined by (11). Please see the plot of a type BB orbit in Figure 2 in order to clarify this notation.

Since type BB solutions can be continued above the homoclinic orbit to (−π2,0)≡(π2,0)(-\frac{\pi}{2},0)\equiv(\frac{\pi}{2},0) in {y>0}\{y>0\} it is natural to consider the orbit parametrized by the ordinate of one of its points. It turns out that, from the computational point of view, an appropriate parameter is the square of the ordinate y⁡(−L)y(-L) of the initial point of the orbit. We shall denote this parameter by zz. Using V⁡(−ϕ,z)=V⁡(−α,0)V(-\phi,\sqrt{z})=V(-\alpha,0), we can obtain the expression for TBT_{B} from (9) when the orbit is bounded by the homoclinics and extended to larger values of zz as explained in Section 2. We thus have

(14) TB(z,ϕ)=∫0ϕ(z−cos2ϕ+cos2x)−1/2dx+∫0x¯⋆​(z)(z−cos2ϕ+cos2x)−1/2dxT_{B}(z,\phi)=\int_{0}^{\phi}(z-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2x)^{-1/2}dx+\int_{0}^{\bar{x}^{\star}(z)}(z-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2x)^{-1/2}dx

where z∈[0,2],z\in[0,2], ϕ∈(0,π2)\phi\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}), and x¯⋆​(z)\bar{x}^{\star}(z) is the function x⋆x^{\star} expressed in the new variable zz, defined above in (12).

Proposition 2.

∂TB∂z​(z,ϕ)⟶−∞\frac{\partial T_{B}}{\partial z}(z,\phi)\longrightarrow-\infty as z→0.z\to 0.

Lemma 1.

∫0x¯⋆​(z)(z−cos2ϕ+cos2x)−3/2dx=O(z12)asz→0.{\displaystyle{\int_{0}^{\bar{x}^{\star}(z)}(z-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2x)^{-3/2}dx}}=O\bigl(z^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\quad\text{as}\quad z\to 0.

Proof.

Since 1−cos⁡2​ϕ=z−cos⁡2​ϕ+cos⁡2​x⋆​(z)<z−cos⁡2​ϕ+cos⁡2​x<z+2,1-\cos 2\phi=z-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2x^{\star}(z)<z-\cos 2\phi+\cos 2x<z+2, and using (17), we get, as z→0z\to 0,

Proposition 3.

The results of Propositions 2 and 4 imply that the time taken by a solution of type BB close to the bifurcation point is smaller than the time T∗T^{*} taken by the critical solution γ⋆\gamma^{\star}.

Actually, for the study of type BB solutions it would have been enough to prove that the derivative ∂TB∂z​(z,ϕ)\frac{\partial T_{B}}{\partial z}(z,\phi) is negative for all z⩾0z\geqslant 0 sufficiently small. The fact that it is not just a negative real number is needed for the study of solution branches that correspond to solutions circling the origin kk times, which will be presented in section 5. 4.4. On the global behavior of type BB solutions branch

The result obtained in the previous section for the time taken by a type BB solution is of a local character: it is valid when the type BB orbit is close to the critical one γ∗,\gamma^{*}, i.e., when the value of the parameter indexing the orbit (be it α\alpha, β\beta, or y⁡(−L)y(-L)) is sufficiently close to the value of the corresponding one in the critical orbit (ϕ\phi, ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}, or 00, resp.).

From the study presented in Section 3 we concluded that the type BB branch of solutions can be continued away from the neighborhood of the critical orbit, and solutions in this branch, parametrized by the value of y⁡(−L)y(-L) only cease to exist when the parameter value is y⁡(−L)=2.y(-L)=\sqrt{2}. To understand the global behavior of this branch for y⁡(−L)∈(0,2)y(-L)\in(0,\sqrt{2}) we need to know the behavior of y⁡(−L)↦TB​(y⁡(−L))y(-L)\mapsto T_{B}(y(-L)). In particular, if we prove that this function is convex, we conclude that the branch of type BB solutions has a unique saddle-node point in the bifurcation diagram.

Unfortunately, despite repeated efforts, we were unable to rigorously establish the positivity of Φ\Phi illustrated in Figure 6, and hence the convexity of z↦TB​(z,ϕ)z\mapsto T_{B}(z,\phi). Alternative approaches to prove the existence of a single minimum of the graph of z↦TB​(z,ϕ)z\mapsto T_{B}(z,\phi), based on attempting to define different type of time maps via changes of variables [3, 5] or other analytic approaches [3] where fruitless.

Thus, we state the following

For each ϕ∈(0,π2),\phi\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}), the function z↦TB​(z,ϕ)z\mapsto T_{B}(z,\phi) is convex.

For the remainder of this paper we assume this conjecture to hold.

4.5. Behavior of type AA solutions branch

From (8) we know that solutions of type AA satisfy TA​(α)=2​T​(α)−TB​(α).T_{A}(\alpha)=2T(\alpha)-T_{B}(\alpha). By the results of section 4.3, we know that TBT_{B} is decreasing when α>ϕ\alpha>\phi close to ϕ\phi, and, by Proposition 1, TT is always increasing. Thus, we conclude that the time TAT_{A} taken by solutions of type AA close to the bifurcation point is larger than the time T∗T^{*} taken by the critical solution γ⋆\gamma^{\star}.

By putting together all previous (analytical and numerical) results we conclude that the bifurcation diagram of (2)–(3) about T∗T^{*} is the one shown in Figure 7.

5. Other bifurcations

As was the case of system (2) with non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions studied in [1, 2], in the present system (2)–(3) with large values of LL we can have solutions turning several times around the origin in the region of the cylindrical phase space bounded by the two homoclinic orbits.

To study these cases we use the same principle of perturbing critical orbits γk∗\gamma^{*}_{k} defined as γ∗\gamma* (i.e., satisfying, in addition to (3), homogeneous boundary conditions y⁡(−L)=0y(-L)=0 and x⁡(L)=0x(L)=0) but now turning kk times around the origin. We have also four distinct types of solutions that we can denote by IkI_{k}, AkA_{k}, BkB_{k} and CkC_{k}, analogous to I,A,BI,A,B and CC, which can be considered the cases with k=0k=0 (i.e., orbits that do not have any complete turn around the origin). The time spent by these orbits with zz sufficiently close to zero is obtained by adding 4​k​T​(α)4kT(\alpha) to the times spent by the corresponding k=0k=0 orbits, e.g.

(31) TIk​(z,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{I_{k}}(z,\phi) =4​k​T​(z)+TI0​(z,ϕ),\displaystyle=4kT(z)+T_{I_{0}}(z,\phi),

and likewise for the other types of orbits.

To build a global picture of the IkI_{k} solution branch as zz increases away from z=0z=0 we need to start by recalling what happens with the II branch (i.e.: with the case k=0k=0). This was studied in sections 3 and 4.1, and illustrated in figures 3 and 7: the II branch of solutions collapses to a single point and disappears when z=ϕ⋆z=\sqrt{\phi^{\star}}.

In the case of IkI_{k} with k⩾1k\geqslant 1 an entirely different behaviour takes place: the IkI_{k} branch of solutions exists for all z<z⋆:=1+cos⁡2​ϕz<z^{\star}:=1+\cos 2\phi, where z⋆z^{\star} is the value of zz of the point on the homoclinic orbit with x=−ϕx=-\phi, and TIk​(z)→+∞T_{I_{k}}(z)\to+\infty when z→z⋆.z\to z^{\star}. In fact we have the two situations we now describe:

Suppose ϕ∈(π4,π2)\phi\in\bigl(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr), then cos⁡2​ϕ<0\cos 2\phi<0 and thus z⋆=1+cos⁡2​ϕ<1−cos⁡2​ϕ=(ϕ⋆)2z^{\star}=1+\cos 2\phi<1-\cos 2\phi=(\phi^{\star})^{2} which implies that the point where the branch of solutions of type II collapse, P⋆=(−ϕ,ϕ⋆)P^{\star}=(-\phi,\phi^{\star}) in Figure 3, is above the point (−ϕ,z⋆)(-\phi,z^{\star}) at the homoclinic. This implies that, as z↑z⋆z\uparrow z^{\star}, the orbits of type IkI_{k} converge to the homoclinic net constituted by the point (−π2,0)≡(π2,0)\bigl(-\frac{\pi}{2},0\bigr)\equiv\bigl(\frac{\pi}{2},0\bigr) and the two homoclinic orbits, as illustrated in Figure 8. The time spent will, obviously, converge to +∞+\infty.

Assume now ϕ∈(0,π4)\phi\in\bigl(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr). Then cos⁡2​ϕ>0\cos 2\phi>0 and thus z⋆=1+cos⁡2​ϕ>1−cos⁡2​ϕ=(ϕ⋆)2z^{\star}=1+\cos 2\phi>1-\cos 2\phi=(\phi^{\star})^{2} which implies that the point P⋆P^{\star} is now located inside the homoclinic net, as illustrated in Figure 9. It is clear from this figure that the time spent by these type of orbits IkI_{k} is given by

(32) TIk​(z,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{I_{k}}(z,\phi) =4​k​T​(z)−TI0​(z,ϕ).\displaystyle=4kT(z)-T_{I_{0}}(z,\phi).

From Proposition 1, section 4.1, and from V⁡(−α,0)=V⁡(−ϕ,z)V(-\alpha,0)=V(-\phi,\sqrt{z}), which results in the relation α=12​arccos⁡(cos⁡2​ϕ−z)\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\arccos(\cos 2\phi-z), it is easy to conclude that orbits whose time map is given by (32) satisfy

(33) ∂TIk∂z​(z,ϕ)\displaystyle\frac{\partial T_{I_{k}}}{\partial z}(z,\phi) >0\displaystyle>0

and hence the corresponding solution branch in the bifurcation diagram is the graph of a monotonic increasing function converging to the horizontal asymptote z=z⋆z=z^{\star} as the time LL converges to +∞+\infty.

In the other hand, for orbits IkI_{k} that do not enclose the point P⋆P^{\star} (i.e., those illustrated in Figure 8), the computation of ∂TIk∂z​(z,ϕ)\frac{\partial T_{I_{k}}}{\partial z}(z,\phi) faces exactly the same problems as we confronted in section 4.4 for the global behaviour of solution branch BB.

Actually, we can repeat the arguments in section 4.3 to conclude that ∂TIk∂z​(z,ϕ)→−∞\frac{\partial T_{I_{k}}}{\partial z}(z,\phi)\to-\infty as z→0z\to 0. Since, as we noted above, TIk​(z,ϕ)→+∞T_{I_{k}}(z,\phi)\to+\infty as z→z⋆z\to z^{\star}, we conclude that the TIk​(z,ϕ)T_{I_{k}}(z,\phi) must have at least one minimum for some22 2 Observe that, due to (33), if the interval (ϕ⋆,z⋆)(\phi^{\star},z^{\star}) is not empty the piece of the solution branch IkI_{k} with zz in this interval is monotonic and so the minima of the IkI_{k} branch must necessarily correspond to values z<ϕ⋆z<\phi^{\star}. z∈(0,ϕ⋆)z\in(0,\phi^{\star}). A numerical study entirely analogous the one presented in section 4.4 allows us to believe that Conjecture 1 is also valid for the branches IkI_{k} with k⩾1k\geqslant 1.

From the fact that the time maps for the branches BkB_{k} with k⩾1k\geqslant 1 are, like in (31), obtained from the one of branch BB by adding 4​k​T​(z)4kT(z), the conclusion we reached for the branches IkI_{k} is repeated for the BkB_{k}s.

Thus, from the discussion above and assuming Conjecture 1 holds true for the branches IkI_{k} and BkB_{k} with k⩾1k\geqslant 1, the bifurcation scheme for the solution branches with k⩾1k\geqslant 1 is shown in Figure 10.

Additional to these orbits, there are another two families of orbits, that we denote by DkD_{k} and Dk′D_{k}^{\prime}, which correspond to orbits analogous to BB and B′B^{\prime} but are located above the homoclinic orbit with positive yy-component, and turn around the cylindrical phase space kk times (see example in Figure 11).

The amount of time spent by these orbits are given by

(34) TDk​(z,ϕ)\displaystyle T_{D_{k}}(z,\phi) :=2​k​T1​(z,π2)+T1​(z,ϕ)+T1​(z,x¯⋆​(z))\displaystyle:=2kT_{1}\bigl(z,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\bigr)+T_{1}(z,\phi)+T_{1}(z,\bar{x}^{\star}(z))

We can see directly from Figure 11 that when z=2z=2 the end points of DkD_{k} and Dk′D_{k}^{\prime} are the same (and coincide with the point (π2,ϕ⋆)(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\phi^{\star}).) This can also be obtained from (34)-(35):

From (36) we conclude that, for each kk, the branches DkD_{k} and Dk′D_{k}^{\prime} exist for all z∈(z⋆,2)z\in(z^{\star},2) and, in a bifurcation diagram with time as the bifurcation variable and zz as the dependent variable, the DkD_{k} branch will always be to the left of the Dk′D_{k}^{\prime}, except at one single point, with ordinate z=2z=2, where they coincide.

To study the monotonicity of the branches DkD_{k} and Dk′D_{k}^{\prime} we again use the time maps (34) and (35), respectively. The last is easier: differentiating (35) with respect to zz we obtain, after some algebraic manipulations,

The existence of a unique minimum of TDk​(⋅,ϕ)T_{D_{k}}(\cdot,\phi) can be checked numerically like was done in the case of the BB branch in section 4.4, but, as there, the rigorous proof eludes us at present. All numerical evidence points to the validity of Conjecture 1 also for the function z↦TDk​(z,ϕ),z\mapsto T_{D_{k}}(z,\phi), and assuming this the situation with branches DkD_{k} and Dk′D_{k}^{\prime} is illustrated in Figure 12.

6. Conclusion

Gathering the results and discussions from the previous sections we can construct the following schematic bifurcation diagram for solutions of (2)–(3).
